cues.text: A watchmaker once turned away from the monastery and a lacemaker once turned away from the convent, Louis and Zélie Martin found each other.
In marriage itself, they found the vocation to holiness each had originally sought elsewhere.
Married in 1858 after a courtship of only a few months, they raised nine children in a home saturated with ordinary daily prayer.
Five surviving daughters entered religious life, including the youngest, whom the world would come to know as St. Thérèse of Lisieux.
Zélie died of breast cancer in 1877.
After years of failing health, including a difficult stay in a sanitarium, Louis followed her in 1894.
He left behind not a single dramatic public deed but an entire household formed, letter by letter and habit by habit, into a school of sanctity.
In 2015, Pope Francis canonized them together, the first married couple in history to be declared saints as a couple.
He held up their homes in Alençon and Lisieux as proof that ordinary family life, rightly lived, is itself a genuine path to God.
